objects.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle
introductoryTalk: Apollo 11's descent stage. Two men rode it down on 20 July 1969.
The ascent stage took them back to Collins and burned up in Earth's air. This half stayed.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

briefing.q: Why is only half a spacecraft here?
briefing.a: It is two stages. The bottom half is legs, tankage and the descent engine; the top half is the cockpit. Only the top could leave, so only the top did. Six modules landed on the Moon and six descent stages are still out there.
The program flew most of it. At 600 m Armstrong saw the target was a boulder field and took the hand. He flew east over it and set down with about twenty-five seconds of propellant to spare.

Executive alarms. The rendezvous radar was loading the computer's bus faster than it could schedule the landing. Steve Bales at Guidance called them executable - keep going. Aldrin cleared them one at a time.

briefing.q: How did the ground take it?
briefing.a: Soft. The pads punched into the fines about half their depth and the engine scoured a dark halo you can see from orbit. There is no wind here to smooth it. The footprints are still exactly where they were put down.

A seismometer and a laser reflector - the first instruments set down on another world - plus a flag and 45 kg of refuse. They left the refuse on purpose. The ascent had to lift two men and a sample box, and every gram came out of the same margin.

Yes. Observatories still range the Moon off it, bouncing a pulse across 380,000 km to the centimetre. It is the weakest of the five arrays left up here and still returns a handful of photons per shot.

Twenty-two weeks. The sun climbed over Tranquility and the electronics, designed for a year, cooked. Every Apollo surface station ended the same way: heat, dust, or somebody in Houston turning it off to save money.
Not upright. The ascent stage's exhaust laid it down; orbiters have seen it in the dust beside the legs since 2012. The other five flags are still standing, as far as anyone can resolve from orbit.

briefing.q: Was this site ever visited again?
briefing.a: No. Twelve men walked on the Moon and every mission went somewhere new. The six sites are six different latitudes. Tranquility has been photographed from orbit many times and touched by nobody since 1969.
Not with what is here. The descent engine burned once, and its tanks were vented after liftoff. It was never a launch pad. It is the scaffolding a launch pad rode down on.
Nothing in law protects it. A 2020 US direction tells American missions to keep their distance; nobody else is bound. The real protection is that nobody can afford to come.
Millions of years, minus micrometeorites. No water, no oxygen, no wind, no biology - and the only vibration is a quake. The plaque on the strut will be legible longer than any book in print.

A dark blast halo, the lander and its shadow, the flag lying down, and the discards exactly where they were dropped. Half a tonne of hardware, a hundred boots of track, and two men who went home the only way they could.

"Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind." It is bolted to a strut of the descent stage, so it is still facing the same way it did in 1969.

The ladder, the survey camera, overshoes, the portable life support backing, a gas analzer, food, waste. The list is in the mission report, and it is a list of people deciding what a return ticket is worth.

briefing.q: What part of it is most human?
briefing.a: The ladder. It was jettisoned on the way up, because the stage was heavy and the ascent had to be margined. So Eagle came down with a way to climb down and left without one.

objects.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Rover 1
introductoryTalk: Rover 1. 210 kg of aluminium tubing and four wire-mesh wheels: the first vehicle anybody drove on another world.
Scott and Irwin drove it 27.8 km in three hours and two minutes, then parked it 160 m from the lander and walked away.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

QA.location: Hadley-Apennine, the VIP parking spot about 160 m from Falcon · 26.1324°N 3.6333°E

briefing.q: Did it have a steering wheel?
briefing.a: No. A T-shaped hand controller on the armrest between the seats: push it forward to go, pull back to stop. All the way back it is the parking brake. No key, no gearbox: four Delco motors, a quarter horsepower each, geared 80 to one.

27.8 km in three hours and two minutes of driving, which is about nine kilometres an hour averaged over the stops. The longest single traverse was 12.5 km, and the farthest they got from this machine on any day was 5.0 km.

briefing.q: What were the wheels made of?
briefing.a: Woven zinc-coated steel cable, 81.8 cm across and 23 cm wide, formed over aluminium discs with titanium chevrons. Inside hung a 64.8 cm bump-stop frame, so a rock bent the mesh instead of the vehicle. GM called it the resilient wheel.

briefing.q: How did they find their way back?
briefing.a: A directional gyro and an odometer on the front bulkhead: what let two men drive 5 km out and come straight back. The gyro drifted. Then they set heading on the Sun-shadow device, a disc you turned until the Sun's edge filled a slot.

Two 36-volt silver-zinc batteries, 121 ampere-hours each, non-rechargeable, in a bay under the floor panels. They were sized to be flat at the end of the third traverse. This machine was spent hardware by design, agreed before launch.

briefing.q: Why does it fold in half?
briefing.a: Because the Lunar Module's Quadrant 1 bay is a box about five feet square, and a rover only fits if it collapses. Three sections on centre hinges, folded flat, then unfolded on the surface by pulling ropes on pulleys and braked reels.

briefing.q: Was there a camera on it?
briefing.a: A television camera on the nose, plugged into the rover's 36-volt outlet and steered from Earth by somebody in Arizona. It was parked facing the lander to film the liftoff. The operator lost the ascent stage in the frame; Apollo 17 got it right.

briefing.q: How did it not cook its own motors?
briefing.a: Wax. Heat capacitors under the deck boiled it, and upward-facing radiators threw the heat off into the sky. While it was driven the radiators were blanketed with mylar, so the wax stayed molten and the gearboxes stayed in tolerance.

briefing.topic: Why it is still standing here
briefing.a: Nothing on it failed. It drove at the end of the third traverse as well as it had at the start of the first, and it was left. There was no reason to fly 210 kg back. It is the rare machine in this story abandoned while it still worked.

briefing.topic: Why it is still standing here
briefing.q: Why park it on that spot?
briefing.a: The crew called it the VIP site. They set the rover down facing the lander so its camera could watch the ascent stage go up. LROC puts it 160 m east of the descent stage in one caption and southeast in another. Neither has moved in fifty years.

briefing.topic: Why it is still standing here
briefing.q: Was any of it a first?
briefing.a: The first wheeled vehicle driven off Earth, the first 12 km traverse on another world, and a 2.4 m core drilled by the ALSEP. And the first hammer-and-feather drop where there is no air. They landed together, which is what Galileo could only argue about.

briefing.topic: Why it is still standing here
briefing.q: Can you still see it from orbit?
briefing.a: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter came over at 27 centimetres a pixel and published it on the fiftieth anniversary of the landing. Lander, ALSEP, this rover, the dark track lines to the rille, and Scott's footprints annotated where he left them.

briefing.topic: What they took and what they left
briefing.a: A plate on the chassis: Man's First Wheels on the Moon, Delivered by Falcon, July 30, 1971. Falcon is the lander 160 m off. Apollo 15 was the first mission to name its two vehicles separately.

briefing.topic: What they took and what they left
briefing.q: What did they find at the rille?
briefing.a: Genesis Rock, sample 15415: pale anorthosite from the highland crust, at least 4.1 billion years old, taken at Station 4. And Great Scott, a 9.6 kg boulder by the rille, too interesting to leave and too heavy to carry off casually.

briefing.topic: What they took and what they left
briefing.a: An aluminium figure eight centimetres tall and a list of fourteen dead, American and Soviet, posed in front of the lander. The sculptor made a hundred. Ninety-nine went to families. NASA had not approved the one that flew in a suit pocket.

briefing.topic: What they took and what they left
briefing.q: Did they have to lie to get a sample?
briefing.a: Yes. David Scott told the camera his seatbelt had caught, walked off, and came back with a rock nobody had asked for. It was the first lunar sample with visible holes in it, and it is catalogued under the lie: Seatbelt Basalt.

objects.name: Surveyor 3
introductoryTalk: Surveyor 3. Robotic, twelve years before the first human boot, and the only probe a human being has ever walked up to.
It landed in April 1967 and died of night. Apollo 12 came for it in 1969.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

QA.location: Southeast Oceanus Procellarum, inside a 200 m subdued crater · 3.0162°S 23.4180°W

briefing.a: It came down on a 14 degree slope inside a shallow crater, and its three footpads did not land on the same surface. The site had been chosen from orbit as the flattest available ground. It was still not flat.

Three times. The vernier engines kept firing through the first touchdown and lifted it off again. The first and second contacts were 20 m apart; the second and third 11 m. It slid another 30 cm before it settled.

Somebody on Earth. An engine-cutoff command was transmitted 34 seconds after the first touchdown. A probe that could not be trusted to switch itself off was landed by a human being pressing a button from 380,000 km away.

briefing.q: How did it survive the hop?
briefing.a: The legs were hollow fibreglass crushable struts, deliberately designed to fail so the body would not. They punched the pads in to half their depth and the spacecraft stayed upright for two weeks of daylight.

briefing.q: Why did the landing matter so much?
briefing.a: Before Surveyor, serious people thought a spacecraft might sink into lunar dust up to its radio mast. The sampler dug trenches 18 cm deep and reported bearing strength. Apollo's legs were sized against that number.

A claw on a three-axis arm, scooping and dropping soil in front of the camera to read its texture and cohesion. It worked for 18 hours and 22 minutes and it is the ancestor of every robotic arm NASA has landed since.
6,326, each one a slow scan of a mechanical television system, transmitted as dots to a dish in the desert. The last frames were of a sunset and a shadow crossing the frame.

briefing.q: What did it see of the Earth?
briefing.a: It photographed an eclipse of the Sun by the Earth, in April 1967, from a spacecraft sitting in a crater. That is a picture of our planet as a disc taking a bite out of the Sun, taken before any human being left orbit.
Data stopped on 4 May 1967 at 00:04 UT, at local sunset, exactly as designed. It was built to survive one lunar night, and only one.

briefing.q: Why did it not wake up?
briefing.a: The batteries and the electronics were not rated for minus 150 degrees, and there was no heater with enough power. It did not come back at the next dawn, and nobody expected it to.

No. It returned 6,326 images and the mechanical properties of the lunar surface, which was the mission. Abandoned hardware that finished its job is a different thing from a failure, and this one is still standing where it worked.
Seven Surveyors flew between 1966 and 1968; five landed, and Surveyor 3 was the first to soften down intact. The programme cost 469 million dollars and was over before Apollo 11's crew had flown.

briefing.topic: The only probe with a visitor
briefing.q: What did the astronauts do to it?
briefing.a: Conrad and Bean came over on their second moonwalk, photographed it, opened it, and sawed off the camera and a piece of scoop. They handled 1.6 m of their own spacecraft's history with a hand tool.

briefing.topic: The only probe with a visitor
briefing.a: In a museum on Earth, with lunar dust still in its mechanism, having been flown home and examined in a clean room. It is the only object that has been on the Moon, taken off, and put in a display case.

briefing.topic: The only probe with a visitor
briefing.a: A disc of goodwill messages from 73 nations, left on the Moon by Apollo 11 near here and not near this. The nearest thing anyone has ever left up here that was intended as a message rather than equipment.

briefing.topic: The only probe with a visitor
briefing.q: Would we go back for it?
briefing.a: It would be easier to land a new spacecraft than to drive 4,000 km across the Moon to this one. Which is the argument for leaving things where they fell, and pointing a camera at them from orbit instead.

objects.name: Apollo 16 ALSEP
introductoryTalk: Not a vehicle. A seismometer, a magnetometer, a solar-wind collector and a plutonium battery, left running for five years.
Apollo 16 turned it on at 19:38 UT on 21 April 1972. On 30 September 1977 Mission Control set it to standby and never woke it.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

briefing.q: What powers a station on the Moon?
briefing.a: A SNAP-27: about 70 watts at 16 volts from a plutonium-238 fuel element. NASA compared it to a light bulb, and under. It was built for two years. Every unit in the network ran between five and eight.

Apollo 11 tried sunlight. Its seismometer worked only in daylight, and it died at 21 days. The lunar night is fourteen days at minus 170. Nothing solar gets through it, so everything after carried radioisotope power.

The fuel element flew in a cask forged to survive a launch failure, a re-entry and an impact, and it was tested on all three. It was set downwind so its vent gas could not coat the experiments. Apollo 12's crew felt the cask's heat through their gloves.

briefing.q: How far apart were the instruments?
briefing.a: Apollo 12's station went in about 90 m from its lander. The portable magnetometer stood on a tripod 15 m from the rover. What LROC sees here is a station, a generator, a rover, and a line of geophones running west, each a dark mark in the soil.

briefing.q: Why put a seismometer on the Moon?
briefing.a: The Moon is not quiet: shallow quakes from tidal stress, quakes from impacts, and deep moonquakes that repeat on a schedule. Apollo 12's station heard the Apollo 13 lander crashed into the Moon 72 km away, and it rang like a bell for 55 minutes.

The Active Seismic Experiment fired small charges from a mortar and hit the ground with a thumper, to read the layers below. Three of four mortar charges went before the pitch sensor ran off scale, and 19 of 22 thumper shots. For a first try, enough.

briefing.q: Why are the magnetometer arms gold?
briefing.a: Gold Kapton on the arms of a ring-core magnetometer, stood on a tripod away from the station's own metal. It found no global field. That is why the solar wind arrives here unshielded, and why the soil at your feet is hungry for it.

briefing.q: What happened to the heat flow experiment?
briefing.a: Two probes went in, one shallow and one drilled deep. John Young caught his foot on the cable and pulled the deep one out. It was not broken. It was unplugged mid-traverse with other work to do, and the experiment was terminated rather than repaired.

Money. NASA ended ALSEP support on 30 September 1977, in its own words, due primarily to budgetary considerations. By then the power pack of at least one station could not run its transmitter and any experiment at the same time.

Five stations ran against a one-year design life, and that network is still the only seismic array on another world. Their transmitters were deliberately left on. JPL needed fixed points on a moving rock for geodesy and navigation.

Between 18 October and 28 November 1977, after the American missions were over, the Soviet RATAN-600 listened to all five. They were still radiating because the navigation transmitters had never been shut down. Somebody in the Crimea used it.

briefing.q: Is any of it still alive?
briefing.a: Nothing here is switched on and nothing here can be. The generator is a cold lump of plutonium fifty years past warranty. It keeps its position to well under a metre, which is why the transmitters ran on long after the science stopped.

Descartes Highlands, 8.9754 degrees south, 15.4981 degrees east, on the far south-east of the near side. Between two young craters, North Ray a kilometre across and South Ray 680 m, which had dug the bedrock up for them.

A geologist in Lunar Orbiter photographs found unusually bright ground here and argued it must be volcanic. Most agreed. It was not. Descartes is impact breccia, blown up, fallen back and welded by collisions. That surprise is the mission.
John Young and Charlie Duke, three days in April 1972, with Ken Mattingly overhead in Casper. They took back 95.71 kg of this ground, the second-heaviest load ever flown off the Moon.

The rover. Young knocked its rear fender extension off at Station 8, and soil turned up on the instruments all mission. Apollo 15's rover had no extensions at all. Complaints produced them, and the crews after him lost them again.

objects.name: Sojourner, at the Carl Sagan Memorial Station
introductoryTalk: Eleven and a half kilograms, the size of a milk crate, beside the lander it came down in. The smallest thing NASA ever drove.
It landed on 4 July 1997, rolled off a ramp on the second sol, and worked for eighty-three sols against a plan of eight.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

briefing.a: Its parachute opened at 370 metres a second, supersonic in thin air, and dragged it down to 68. Rockets did the rest. Three gas generators filled the airbag skirt 355 m up, in under a second. Then it bounced and rolled until it stopped.

Because this is a flood channel strewn with boulders, and a legged lander on a boulder ends up tipped over and blind. Airbags do not care what they hit. Four winches on the petals pulled the bags back in against the lander once it was up.

They are not ramps, they are the solar arrays: three petals folded from vertical to horizontal, 87 minutes after landing. The cells were on the inside of the petals, which is the same face as the top of the ramp. Dust had them within a sol.

briefing.q: Why is the lander a memorial?
briefing.a: Once it had landed safe, NASA renamed the lander the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, after the astronomer. The rover's name came from a schools contest with 3,500 entries, won by a twelve-year-old asking for Sojourner Truth.

Thirteen centimetres of aluminium wheel, six of them, on a rocker and a bogie with no axles and no springs to jam. The bogie ties the front wheel to the middle, the rocker carries the rear pair, so it stays level over an 8 cm rock.

Neither. A flip-up stereo camera head at each end and a colour camera on the back, and it decided as it went. Each front camera had five laser stripe projectors: it lit the ground with stripes and measured the hole before driving in.

briefing.q: How much power does it have?
briefing.a: One flat array on its back, thirteen strings of gallium-arsenide cells, over the gold box the batteries lived in. Lander and rover had about a kilowatt-hour a day: two to four hours of talking, and enough warmth to keep its memory.

An Alpha-Proton X-ray Spectrometer on a little deployment arm, reading an element by what a source throws back. It had to sit exactly one reach from the target, so the rover came at every rock in steps of a wheel diameter.

briefing.q: Why land in a flood channel?
briefing.a: Water had done the sampling already. Everything the flood could move from upstream was carried into this field. Land once, read a whole catchment. It was also a cheap test for a rover: a field of obstacles for eight sols of cover.

Two rocks here, Barnacle Bill and Yogi, came back as andesite, which on Earth means crust that has been worked over. That was unwelcome. Andesite takes a step between mantle and crust, and Mars was supposed to be too simple for it.

briefing.q: Was it a surprise to anybody?
briefing.a: An eight-sol technology demonstration that did geology for eighty-three and never stopped working to do it. The first wheeled vehicle on another world, and its lander's windsocks were the first Martian weather since Viking.

briefing.q: How far did it actually drive?
briefing.a: Its radio reached 500 m, and that number keeps being repeated as how far it drove. It is how far it could talk. NASA never published an odometer total. The tracks, photographed by the lander and later by HiRISE, are the only one.

The last transmission from this site was received at 10:23 UT on 27 September 1997, ninety-two sols after it arrived. Communications failed for good after 7 October, on a sol the lander was expected to talk.

Formally, unknown. NASA's own line is that contact was lost for reasons that were never established. Dust on the arrays was suspect one; a heater stuck on and draining the batteries in the cold was suspect two.

briefing.q: Did they try to bring it back?
briefing.a: Five months of it. Commands, rehearsals on the test article in the sandbox at JPL, then termination on 10 March 1998. A flight spare of this rover is in a museum on Earth, still wired, still running the software that drove it here.

briefing.q: Can you see any of it now?
briefing.a: HiRISE came over in January 2007 and put the lander down as a bright mark with three ramps and moved soil around it. The rover is too small to pick out. But Big Crater, the landmark its mast camera photographed, is there, 3 km off.

objects.name: Opportunity
introductoryTalk: Opportunity. The other one, and the one that is still out there with its wheels in the sand of Jezero's neighbourhood.
It was certified for 90 sols. It drove 45.16 kilometres in nearly fifteen years and died of a dust storm.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

QA.location: Perseverance Valley, west rim of Endeavour Crater, Meridiani Planum · 2.28°S 5.23°W

briefing.a: 1.9483 degrees south, 354.4742 degrees east, in a 20-metre crater at Meridiani Planum, 14.9 km from the aim point. That site is now called Challenger Memorial Station.
At least 26. It dropped out of the aeroshell at terminal velocity, hit the ground at walking pace and skipped. The airbag system was tested by dropping it off a tower until it stopped breaking.

briefing.q: What was the first thing it saw?
briefing.a: Ground so full of small grey spheres that the first week was spent explaining that they were concretions, not fossils. They had formed in water, which was the point of being there.

briefing.q: Was the landing site chosen for the rocks?
briefing.a: Yes. Orbiters found hematite - which on Earth precipitates out of water - spread over an area too large to sample on foot. The problem with landing on a promising plain is that you can walk 45 km and still be on it.

briefing.q: How far did it actually drive?
briefing.a: 28.06 miles, 45.16 kilometres, at an average of about 35 metres a sol. That is still the longest distance any wheeled vehicle has driven on another world.

A 22-km crater whose rim had been excavated from under the sand sheet, so it exposed older rock. It took Opportunity eight months and a great deal of luck to reach it, and it spent the rest of its life on that rim.

On distance, yes. On everything else, no - Spirit found the silica, and both rovers found the same thing that mattered. They were twins with one design and one software bug, and each was the other's backup.

briefing.q: How did it keep working so long?
briefing.a: Its panels stayed cleaner than anyone predicted; dust storms on Mars clean as well as cover. And the rover was allowed to sleep through bad weather instead of dying in it.
In a gully on the eastern rim of Endeavour, on a slope of 15 to 17 degrees, facing down the hill. The team had named it Perseverance Valley a year before it got there, from an orbit photo.
Sol 5111, 10 June 2018. Its last telemetry reported 22 watt-hours made and the dustiest sky ever measured on Mars. The opacity reading was 10.8, and it was rising.

briefing.q: How did the storm kill it?
briefing.a: A planet-encircling storm that lasted for months and put enough dust on the panels that the battery never recovered. Cold, dark and no power is exactly the failure mode the designers had listed and accepted.

The last transmission was a set of instrument readings, as always, from a rover that could not see the Sun. The sentence everyone remembers - about a low battery and getting dark - was written by a human being as an epitaph.
In September 2018 the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the valley floor and found it where the last commands put it. Silent, upright, wheels in the sand, panels covered.
A bright speck the size of a car in a shadowed gully, with the tracks leading into it and stopping. It was the first time anyone had confirmed the position of a dead rover by looking down at it.

On 13 February 2019, after more than 800 recovery attempts and a winter of dark skies. The heaters were off and the battery was probably frozen. NASA judged a bad command riskier than the chance of a wake-up.

It died inside Jezero Crater's rim, on the valley where Perseverance would later land to look at the same ancient delta. Two rovers, twenty years apart, working the same crater wall. One is still there.

objects.name: InSight
introductoryTalk: InSight. Not a rover - it never moved after it landed, and that was the design.
It listened to the inside of Mars for four years with a seismometer it had to set down by arm, and a mole that would not dig.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

briefing.a: Because a seismometer cannot measure anything while it is driving. It had to be sitting still, on hard ground, for years. Every marsquake it ever recorded came from a machine that had not moved since the day it touched down.

Parachute, then a rocket-powered back shell that hovered and set it down on three legs, then flew off and crashed 1 km away. That back shell became a free seismometer when it landed. It was heard falling, 1 km from the lander.

Low, flat, sunlit and near the equator, so the solar arrays would keep the batteries warm through a cold winter. The site is a lava plain, chosen for the boringness. Nothing on it was interesting to look at.

briefing.q: What was on the ground with it?
briefing.a: A domed seismometer on the ground, a heat probe on a tether, a radio science package, and a scoop that dug in during week one. The seismometer is still sitting there, still level, still listening to nothing.

briefing.topic: The mole that would not dig
briefing.q: What was HP3 supposed to do?
briefing.a: A self-hammering probe the length of a forearm, designed to burrow 5 metres and read heat coming up from the interior. Five metres is where Mars still holds the record of how it formed.

briefing.topic: The mole that would not dig
briefing.a: The regolith here is dry, coarse and has no cohesion, so the mole rebounded instead of biting. Every hammer blow pushed it back out of its own hole. On Earth you push down; here there is nothing to push against.

briefing.topic: The mole that would not dig
briefing.a: For eighteen months. They built a backstop out of a section of its own tether and pressed it against the mole with the arm. It gained a little. Then the deployment arm began to fail, and the instrument was abandoned in place.

briefing.topic: The mole that would not dig
briefing.a: Forty centimetres of a five-metre design goal, after more than a year of hammering. It is the most expensive hole ever dug on Mars, and it taught the next mission how to anchor.
More than a thousand, over four years, in a place where nobody had heard anything before. Most were tiny. A handful were large enough to make the whole planet ring.

A magnitude-five event on 25 May 2022 - the largest tremor ever measured on another world, two years past its design life. It was recorded by a seismometer that had been left in the open on purpose, because a mole had failed.

briefing.q: What did it learn about the core?
briefing.a: Mars has a liquid core, about 1,830 km in radius, and less dense than anyone expected. That single number settled a debate that had run from Viking to the orbiters, and it came from sound.
Wind. Constantly - the dome was not sealed against it, so the ground noise is part of every record. And it detected meteoroid impacts on the surface, which nobody had measured before.

Dust built up on the arrays until the battery could not keep the electronics warm, and the power fell below the radio's needs. It was the failure mode written into the mission design from the start, and the one thing nobody could clean.
15 December 2022. Two failed attempts to reach it later, on 21 December, the mission was declared over. The last command had been a two-week silence to wait out the dust. The dust did not clear.

Nothing is switched on, but nothing has fallen over either. The deck, the dome, the mole and the tether are all still in place. InSight will sit in Elysium Planitia for millions of years. If a mission needs flat ground to stand on, it is still there.
It delivered the size and state of a planet's core from one fixed spot, on a Discovery-programme budget. It was abandoned because the panels got dirty, not because it stopped answering.

objects.name: Viking 1
introductoryTalk: Viking 1. The first machine that landed on Mars and kept talking, on 20 July 1976 - the country's bicentennial.
It lasted six years and died because of something we sent it.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

briefing.a: Earlier American landers were all lost. Viking 1 came down on 20 July 1976, a month after its orbiter chose the site. It was still operating in 1982, longer than anyone had promised.

Entry, a supersonic parachute, then 24 thrusters flying the last kilometre before the lander dropped out from under them. The lander then had to right itself, deploy three legs and wait for dust to clear before it took a picture.

Chryse Planitia: a stony, wind-scoured plain at 22 degrees north, in ground that looks water-carved from orbit. It was chosen from orbit after the site originally picked was found to be too rough to land on.

briefing.q: What was the plan for life?
briefing.a: Three biology experiments run at once, so no single result could be over-read: label release, gas exchange, gas chromatograph. That design is the reason the argument about the answer has never finished.

It found something like metabolism and something like sterilisation, in the same sample, in the same hour. NASA's own biologists could not agree, so the official result was: inconclusive, and probably chemistry.

The labeled-release test gave off carbon dioxide as if the dirt were eating what was poured on it - then stopped when baked. The gas chromatograph found no organic carbon at all, which is what killed the biological reading.

briefing.q: Why is it still argued about?
briefing.a: Nobody had measured oxidants in Martian soil. When Phoenix found perchlorate in 2008, Viking's results made sense without life. And perchlorate also destroys organics when you bake it, which is exactly what the chromatograph did.
Fifty years later the answer is still that we do not know, and that the instrument was not the wrong one - it was the first one. Every mission since has been designed to not have this problem.

briefing.q: What did it do all that time?
briefing.a: It dug, analysed, weighed the soil, measured wind and temperature, and returned tens of thousands of images. It recorded two full Martian years of weather at one fixed point, and that record is still the reference for the site.

briefing.q: How did it survive the winter?
briefing.a: Heaters, on a plutonium power source, and a mission team that learned to schedule by the Martian calendar before it started. Its electronics were designed for a 90-day surface mission and were expected to die in the first winter. They did not.

The first colour picture taken on another planet: pink sand, a rock and a calibration swatch, deliberately staged. And a bright object crossing the sky in 1978, which was Earth and Phobos in the same frame.
Not one centimetre. It had no wheels and no intention of any. Its tracks were made by its own footpads and by nothing else until the wind moved sand around them.

On 11 November 1982 a software uplink meant to help a tired battery overwrote the data that pointed its antenna at Earth. The dish swung away from Earth, the batteries drained, and the lander went silent at 22 degrees north.

Nobody's, in the sense that matters: the procedure was correct, the tape was long, and a check digit did not exist. It ended the record for the longest surface mission on another planet that Viking had held for six years.

The lander was healthy. Pointing it back at Earth needed a dish and a command, and after two months neither was going to arrive. The spacecraft did not wear out. It was switched off by its own ground crew.

Yes. Orbiters have seen it, and its footprints and the trench from its sampler are still visible in the sand. It is the oldest thing on Mars that a human being operated, and the first thing anyone will see when they get there.

objects.name: Mars Global Surveyor
introductoryTalk: Mars Global Surveyor. An orbiter, so there is no ground here - it is still going round Mars, behind you and above.
It mapped the entire planet for ten years and then went silent in 2006 after a command from Earth.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

QA.location: Near-polar Mars orbit, about 450 km up · periapsis 372.8 km, apoapsis 436.5 km

briefing.a: The first global topographic map of another planet, at a resolution that made Mars a place with elevations instead of outlines. Plus a magnetic map, a thermal map and a gravity field good enough to weigh the deep interior.

About 1.4 metres per pixel, and the imaging team picked its own targets: a camera flown by scientists rather than a pilot. Its pictures found gullies so fresh that they had to have formed within the last few years.

A laser rangefinder that fired 5 Hz at the ground for nine years, building a digital elevation model of the whole planet. Every elevation you have ever seen quoted for Mars - Olympus, Hellas, Jezero's rim - is measured against MGS.

briefing.q: Why did it matter for rovers?
briefing.a: It picked the landing sites. Gusev and Meridiani - where Spirit and Opportunity sit - were chosen out of its data. It also imaged the ellipses for the rovers that came after, including the one you just walked past.

Stripes. Crustal remanent magnetisation in banded patterns in the southern highlands, billions of years old. Mars had a global magnetic field early in its history, and lost it - which is why the atmosphere went and the water left.
It means a planet's dynamo can start and stop, and the surface keeps the record of when. Earth looks like this too. We just cannot read ours through thirty kilometres of rock and ocean.

Layered and gullied terrain that reads as liquid water in geologic recent times, plus polar caps with real structure. Not the discovery of water so much as the proof that the argument about water on Mars was the wrong argument.

It watched dust storms merge until one wrapped the planet, and watched the carbon-dioxide frost advance and retreat each season. The seasonal carbon-dioxide wind field it mapped is what every lander since has had to survive.

briefing.q: How long was it meant to last?
briefing.a: One Mars year of mapping. It ran nearly ten, on three extended missions. Everything on it was expected to die before the second winter.

briefing.q: How did it stay up so long?
briefing.a: It used the upper atmosphere as a brake. For six months it dipped its periapsis to 110 km and let Mars drag on its solar wings. That turned a 54,000 km elliptical capture orbit into a 450 km circle without burning the fuel away.

Aerobraking: trading a little heat and a lot of altitude for a cheaper orbit, over hundreds of passes. It is the reason MGS could carry instruments instead of propellant, and why nearly every orbiter since does it.

It relayed the landers. Rovers on Mars talk to a spacecraft overhead, and MGS carried the traffic for three of them. It was a phone line across 200 million km and it never dropped the connection longer than the Sun allowed.
Early November 2006, after a routine yaw manoeuvre during a software update. The telemetry stopped mid-maneuver. The last images had been returned two days earlier, showing the south polar spring.

Most likely a memory glitch that spun the spacecraft and pointed its arrays the wrong way, so the batteries ran down. A command from Earth was involved. Viking's death, thirty-odd years earlier, was the same shape.
Still in a near-polar orbit at about 450 km, and it will stay there for decades. It is expected to fall out of the sky and reach the surface some time after 2047, wherever its orbit happens to decay.

briefing.q: Would we try to fix it?
briefing.a: It is a dead spacecraft with no thrusters, no fuel and no way to receive a command, in an orbit it cannot change. There is nothing to fix. There is a map it made, which is the part that stays.

objects.name: Pioneer 10
introductoryTalk: Pioneer 10. It went out, and it is still going, and it has been silent since 2003.
There is a gold plate bolted to its side with a man and a woman on it, and nobody is coming to read it.
Ask me anything about it, or move on when you're ready.

QA.location: Interstellar space toward Taurus · 80 AU from the Sun at its last signal

briefing.a: It was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt, the first to fly Jupiter, and the first to leave the planets behind. Launched in March 1972, at Jupiter by December 1973, and beyond the orbit of Neptune by the mid-1980s.

It passed 132,000 km above the cloud tops and took the first close pictures of the largest planet in the Solar System. It also found a radiation belt at Jupiter intense enough to fry electronics, which nearly killed Pioneer 11.

briefing.q: How did it survive the belt?
briefing.a: By pointing its antenna at Earth and driving through the middle, with 12 known asteroids on its track and no way to swerve. Engineers calculated the chance of a catastrophic hit at about one in a million. Nobody argued with the arithmetic afterwards.

About 12 km per second relative to the Sun - roughly 2.5 AU a year, and it has been doing it for 50 years. At that rate a signal takes over eleven hours to reach us, which is why the last one was such a small event.

Two human figures, the Solar System drawn from where the craft is, a hydrogen atom, and the Sun located by fourteen pulsars. Carl Sagan pushed for it, drew it with Frank Drake, and it was machined onto gold-anodised aluminium 152 by 229 mm.

briefing.q: Why a man and a woman?
briefing.a: The figures are drawn neutral, with no clothing, because clothing is cultural and they had no idea who would see it. Sagan's wife Ann Druyan was told the nakedness would be a problem and refused to change it.

briefing.q: Did they intend it to be found?
briefing.a: No. It was a gesture, and dated: the launch year is encoded in binary pulses so any reader could work out how old it was. It will outlast every language it could have been written in.

Pioneer 11 carries the same plate. Both are now silent, both are heading out of the ecliptic, and neither will be recovered. Voyager's records are newer and more generous. Pioneer's plate is the one with a drawing of us on it.

A small persistent Doppler drift in the tracking between 20 and 70 AU, as if the Sun were pulling the spacecraft back. It survived every check for 20 years and became a genuine puzzle, with papers written about modified gravity.

Heat. The radioisotope generators radiate unevenly, mostly aft, and that photon thrust is exactly the missing acceleration. Reconstructing the spacecraft's thermal state from its own telemetry closed the case in 2012. It was engineering all along.

The mission was officially ended in 1997 at 67 AU; a faint carrier was still being picked up until 23 January 2003, at 80 AU. The last decodeable telemetry was a partial frame received from 80.22 AU, in April 2002.

briefing.q: How long will the signal last?
briefing.a: It cannot wake up. The plutonium is cold and the transmitter needs more power than is left. The plaque, though, does not need power. It is good for a billion years, in shade.
No. Space is empty on the scale it is moving through, and it is not decelerating for anything. The chance of intersecting a star in the next million years is essentially zero.

briefing.q: What will it be near next?
briefing.a: In about 90,000 years it passes within three quarters of a light year of a small orange star called HIP 117795. That is the nearest approach it will make to anything for two million years.

briefing.q: Is it the farthest thing we made?
briefing.a: It was, for decades, until Voyager 1 went past it and kept accelerating away. Pioneer 10 is now third, behind Voyagers 1 and 2, and it will never catch either.

briefing.q: What should we do about it?
briefing.a: Nothing. It is unreachable by design, and it was not built to be recovered. It is a monument the way a buoy in an ocean is: out there marking the fact that somebody came this far.
